title: Homer’s birds and serpents foresaw nothing
source_text: Ἀλλὰ καὶ εἴπερ οἰωνοὶ οἰωνοῖς μάχονται (καὶ,) ὥς φησιν ὁ Κέλσος, θείαν φύσιν ἔχοντες οἱ μαντικοὶ ὄρνεις καὶ τὰ (ἄλλα) ἄλογα ζῷα καὶ ἐννοίας τοῦ θείου καὶ πρόγνωσιν περὶ μελλόντων τὰ τοιαῦτα ἑτέροις προεδήλουν· οὔτ᾿ ἂν ἡ καθ᾿ Ὅμηρον στρουθὸς ἐνόσσευσεν ὅπου δράκων ἔμελλεν αὐτὴν καὶ τὰ τέκνα ἀφανίσειν, οὔτ᾿ ἂν ὁ κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν ποιητὴν δράκων οὐκ ἐφυλάξατο ὑπὸ τοῦ ἀετοῦ ληφθῆναι. φησὶ γὰρ ὁ ἐν ποιήσει θαυμαστὸς Ὅμηρος περὶ μὲν τοῦ προτέρου τοιαῦτα· ἔνθ᾿ ἐφάνη μέγα σῆμα· δράκων ἐπὶ νῶτα δαφοινὸς, σμερδαλέος, τὸν δ᾿ αὐτὸς Ὀλύμπιος ἧκε φόωσδε, βωμοῦ ὑπαΐξας πρός ῥα πλατάνιστον ὄρουσεν. ἔνθα δ᾿ ἔσαν στρουθοῖο νεοσσοὶ, νήπια τέκνα, ὄζῳ ἐπ᾿ ἀκροτάτῳ πετάλοις ὑποπεπτηῶτες, ὀκτὼ. ἀτὰρ μήτηρ ἐνάτη ἦν. ἣ τέκε τέκνα. ἔνθ᾿ ὅ γε τοὺς ἐλεεινὰ κατήσθιε τετριγῶτας· μήτηρ δ᾿ ἀμφεποτᾶτο ὀδυρομένη φίλα τέκνα· τὴν δ᾿ ἐλελιξάμενος πτέρυγος λάβεν ἀμφιαχυῖαν. αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ κατὰ τέκν᾿ ἔφαγε στρουθοῖο καὶ αὐτὴν, τὸν μὲν ἀρίζηλον θῆκεν θεὸς, ὅσπερ ἔφηνεν· λᾶαν γάρ μιν θῆκε Κρόνου παῖς ἀγκυλομήτεω. ἡμεῖς δ᾿ ἑσταότες θαυμάζομεν οἷον ἐτύχθη. ὡς οὖν δεινὰ πέλωρα θεῶν εἰσῆλθ᾿ ἑκατόμβας, περὶ δὲ τοῦ δευτέρου ὅτι ὄρνις γάρ σφιν ἐπῆλθε περησέμεναι μεμαῶσιν, αἰετὸς ὑψιπέτης, ἐπ᾿ ἀριστερὰ λαὸν ἐέργων, φοινήεντα δράκοντα φέρων ὀνύχεσσι πέλωρον, ζωὸν. ἔτ᾿ ἀσπαίροντα· ὁ δ᾿ οὔπω λήθετο χάρμης. κόψε γὰρ αὐτὸν ἔχοντα κατὰ στῆθος παρὰ δειρὴν, ἰδνωθεὶς ὀπίσω· ὁ δ᾿ ἀπὸ ἕθεν ἧκε χαμᾶζε. ἀλγήσας ὀδύνῃσι, μέσῳ δ᾿ ἐγκάββαλ᾿ ὁμίλῳ· αὐτὸς δὲ κλάγξας πέτετο πνοιῇς ἀνέμοιο. Τρῶες δ᾿ ἐῤῥίγησαν, ὅπως ἴδον αἰόλον ὄφιν κείμενον ἐν μέσσοισι, Διὸς τέρας αἰγιόχοιο. ἆρ᾿ οὖν ὁ μὲν ἀετὸς ἦν μαντικὸς, ὁ δὲ δράκων, ἐπεὶ καὶ τούτῳ χρῶνται τῷ ζῴῳ οἱ οἰωνοσκόποι, οὐκ ἦν μαντικός; τί δὲ, ἐπεὶ τὸ ἀποκληρωτικὸν εὐέλεγκτόν ἐστιν, οὐχὶ καὶ τὸ ἀμφοτέρους εἶναι μαντικοὺς ἐλεγχθείη ἄν; οὐκ ἂν γὰρ ὁ δράκων ὢν μαντικὸς οὐκ ἐφυλάξατο τάδε τινὰ ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀετοῦ παθεῖν; καὶ ἄλλα δ᾿ ἂν μυρία τοιαῦτα εὕροι τις παραδείγματα, παριστάντα ὅτι οὐ τὰ ζῷα μέν ἐστιν ἐν ἑαυτοῖς ἔχοντα μαντικὴν ψυχήν· ἀλλὰ κατὰ μὲν τὸν ποιητὴν καὶ τοὺς πολλοὺς τῶν ἀνθρώπων αὐτὸς Ὀλύμπιος ἧκε φόωσδε, κατὰ δέ τι σημεῖον καὶ Ἀπόλλων ἀγγέλῳ χρῆται ἱέρακι· „κίρκος“ (γὰρ) „Ἀπόλλωνος“ εἶναι λέγεται „ταχὺς ἄγγελος.“
pass_a_gloss: But also if (εἴπερ) birds of omen (οἰωνοί) fight (μάχονται) with birds of omen, and, as Celsus says (φησιν), the prophetic (μαντικοί) birds (ὄρνεις) and the other irrational (ἄλογα) animals (ζῷα), having (ἔχοντες) divine nature (θείαν φύσιν) and conceptions (ἐννοίας) of the divine (τοῦ θείου) and foreknowledge (πρόγνωσιν) about things to come (μελλόντων), used to foretell (προεδήλουν) such things to others: neither would the sparrow (στρουθός) according to Homer have nested (ἐνόσσευσεν) where a serpent (δράκων) was going to destroy (ἀφανίσειν) her and the young (τέκνα), nor would the serpent according to the same poet not have guarded against (οὐκ ἐφυλάξατο) being taken (ληφθῆναι) by the eagle (ἀετοῦ). For Homer, wonderful (θαυμαστός) in poetry, says about the former such things: [Iliad 2.308-321: great sign (σῆμα); serpent blood-red (δαφοινός) on the back, terrible (σμερδαλέος), whom the Olympian himself sent to the light (φόωσδε); darting from under the altar (βωμοῦ) it rushed to the plane tree; there were the sparrow's nestlings (νεοσσοί), infant young, on the topmost branch, cowering under leaves, eight, and the mother ninth who bore the young; there it devoured them pitiably chirping (τετριγῶτας); the mother flew around lamenting her dear young; coiling it seized her by the wing crying about; when it ate the young and her, the god who showed it made it conspicuous (ἀρίζηλον); for the son of crooked-counselled Cronus made it a stone (λᾶαν); we standing marvelled at what was done; so when dread portents (πέλωρα) of the gods came into the hecatombs]; and about the second that: [Iliad 12.200-209: a bird came upon them eager to cross, high-flying eagle on the left, checking the host, bearing in talons a blood-red monstrous serpent, alive, still writhing (ἀσπαίροντα); it had not yet forgotten battle (χάρμης); it struck him that held it on the breast by the neck, bending back; he let it from him to the ground, pained with pangs, threw it in the midst of the throng; himself screaming (κλάγξας) flew on the breaths of wind; the Trojans shuddered (ἐρρίγησαν) when they saw the glittering (αἰόλον) snake (ὄφιν) lying in the midst, portent (τέρας) of aegis-bearing Zeus]. Was then the eagle prophetic, but the serpent, since augurs (οἰωνοσκόποι) also use this animal, not prophetic? And what, since the arbitrary selection (ἀποκληρωτικόν) is easily refuted (εὐέλεγκτον), would not also the both-being-prophetic be refuted? For the serpent being prophetic would not have failed to guard against suffering these things from the eagle. And one could find ten thousand (μυρία) other such examples (παραδείγματα), showing (παριστάντα) that it is not the animals that have in themselves a prophetic soul (μαντικὴν ψυχήν); but according to the poet and the many (πολλούς) of men 'the Olympian himself sent it to the light', and in some sign (σημεῖον) Apollo too uses a hawk (ἱέρακι) as messenger (ἀγγέλῳ): for the 'falcon (κίρκος)' is said to be 'Apollo's swift messenger'.
pass_b_english: Moreover, if birds of omen fight with birds of omen, and if, as Celsus says, the prophetic birds and the other irrational animals, having a divine nature, notions of the divine and foreknowledge of the future, foretold such things to others, then Homer’s sparrow would not have nested where a serpent was going to destroy her and her young, nor would the serpent in the same poet have failed to guard against being seized by the eagle.

For Homer, so admirable a poet, says this about the first: “Then a great sign appeared: a serpent, blood-red on its back, terrible, which the Olympian himself sent forth into the light, darted out from beneath the altar and sped to the plane tree. There were the young of a sparrow, helpless nestlings, on the topmost bough, cowering under the leaves, eight of them, and the mother that bore them was the ninth. There it devoured them as they chirped piteously, while the mother fluttered round, wailing for her dear young; then, coiling itself, it caught her by the wing as she shrieked around it. But when it had eaten the sparrow’s young and the mother herself, the god who had shown it made it conspicuous; for the son of crooked-counselling Cronus turned it to stone. And we stood and marvelled at what had come to pass. So, when the dread portents of the gods broke in upon the hecatombs…” (Homer, Iliad 2.308–321).

And about the second he says: “For a bird had come upon them as they were eager to cross, an eagle flying high, skirting the host on the left, bearing in its talons a monstrous blood-red serpent, alive and still writhing; and it had not yet forgotten the fight, for it struck its captor on the breast beside the neck, bending itself backward; and the eagle, stung with pain, flung it from him to the ground and cast it down in the midst of the throng, and itself, with a scream, flew off on the blasts of the wind. And the Trojans shuddered when they saw the glittering snake lying in their midst, a portent of Zeus who bears the aegis” (Homer, Iliad 12.200–209).

Was the eagle, then, prophetic, and the serpent not prophetic, although the augurs use this animal too? What, then? Since the arbitrary choice of one over the other is easily refuted, would not the view that both are prophetic be refuted as well? For if the serpent had been prophetic, would it not have guarded against suffering this from the eagle? One could find countless other examples like these, showing that it is not the animals that have in themselves a prophetic soul. Rather, according to the poet and most men, “the Olympian himself sent it forth into the light” (Homer, Iliad 2.309); and in a certain sign Apollo too uses a hawk as his messenger, for the “falcon” is said to be “Apollo’s swift messenger” (Homer, Odyssey 15.526).

choices.choice: 'Again: if birds fight with birds' -> 'Moreover, if birds of omen fight with birds of omen' (ἀλλὰ καί; οἰωνοί kept as omen-birds)
'conceptions of the divine' -> 'notions of the divine' (match 4.88 rendering of ἐννοίαι)
'wonderful in poetry' -> 'so admirable a poet' (calque removed)
'as she cried about it' -> 'as she shrieked around it' (ἀμφιαχυῖαν; 'about' was ambiguous)
'struck the eagle that held it' -> 'struck its captor' (αὐτὸν ἔχοντα, no added noun)
added 'What, then?' for omitted τί δέ; 'it is easy to refute' -> 'is easily refuted' (εὐέλεγκτον)
'at the eagle's hands' -> 'from the eagle' (ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀετοῦ)

Homer citations checked by line: the sparrow portent at Aulis is Iliad 2.308–321 (Origen's quotation stops mid-sentence at 2.321, marked with an ellipsis); the eagle and serpent is Iliad 12.200–209; ‘the Olympian himself sent it forth into the light’ repeats Iliad 2.309; ‘falcon, Apollo's swift messenger’ is Odyssey 15.526. Origen's Homer text has small variants from the vulgate (ὁ δ᾿ οὔπω λήθετο for καὶ οὔ πω λήθετο at 12.203; ἐγκάββαλ᾿ for ἐνὶ κάββαλ᾿ at 12.206); translated as Origen gives them. ἀρίζηλον ('conspicuous') is the reading printed; an ancient variant ἀΐζηλον ('made invisible') is not followed. ‘As Celsus says’ introduces a paraphrase of Celsus's claims (from 4.88), so no quotation marks are used there. Koetschau's supplements (καὶ) and (ἄλλα) are translated. τὸ ἀποκληρωτικόν = the arbitrary picking of one alternative (here: eagle prophetic, serpent not); rendered 'the arbitrary choice of one over the other'. κίρκος rendered 'falcon' and ἱέραξ 'hawk' to keep the two words distinct. No Scripture in this chapter.
